title: When normalized expression cannot recover molecule counts
concept: CP10K normalization removes the row total before applying log1p. The smallest positive value is one molecule only when the original row contains a single-molecule observation. A row whose positive counts share an integer factor loses that factor. Treating its smallest positive value as one therefore returns a scaled-down count row.
question: Why does the first recovered row disagree with the input while its normalized expression is unchanged?
answer: The row [2,4,8] and [1,2,4] have identical proportions. Both produce the same normalized expression; no inverse of that normalized row can distinguish them. The [1,3,5] row has an observed single molecule and is recovered in this example.
limit: Exact recovery in a toy row does not establish recovery for a dataset. Prefer a measured count layer; record the normalization convention and any fractional segmentation counts.
variation: Replace the first input row by [3,6,12], then [1,6,12]. Predict which row is identifiable under this particular decoder.

title: Stochastic rounding without systematic molecule loss
concept: Segmentation or allocation may produce fractional counts. Converting them to integers by truncation systematically lowers their expectation. Stochastic rounding adds a Bernoulli draw for the fractional part, preserving each input's expectation while adding sampling variability. It is a modeling choice, not proof of the true molecular observation process.
question: Which operation preserves 0.2, 0.7, 1.4 and 3.8 on average?
answer: Flooring maps the values to 0, 0, 1 and 3. Across many independent rounds, stochastic rounding approaches the original values. The script measures the maximum empirical mean error and checks it is small at its declared sample size.
limit: Unbiased expectation does not mean every draw is accurate, nor that random rounding is appropriate for every downstream method. Preserve the original fractional layer and record the random seed.
variation: Reduce the number of draws from 100000 to 100. Repeat with several seeds and explain why individual empirical errors grow.

title: Why clipping an additive expression shift changes its mean
concept: A constant shift would move a mean by that constant on an unconstrained real line. Expression predictions must be nonnegative. Applying max(x+d,0) clips some cells and makes the resulting mean a nonlinear function of d. A proposed pseudobulk correction can therefore miss its intended target even when its arithmetic looked exact before clipping.
question: Does subtracting 0.5 from every entry reduce the mean by exactly 0.5 after clipping?
answer: No. The zeros cannot become negative, so their intended decrease disappears. The actual clipped mean exceeds the intended mean. This is a numerical consequence of the transformation, independent of biological interpretation.
limit: The lesson does not prescribe a replacement model. Hurdle, multiplicative, molecule-level and constrained methods make different assumptions that need separate validation.
variation: Change the fraction of zeros, keeping the nonzero values fixed. Plot the difference between intended and clipped means.

title: Spatial support when zero-expression ranks are tied
concept: Many cells have the same zero expression value. A quantile transform that activates some zeros must resolve those ties somehow. Random resolution scatters new detections. A local-support rule places them near cells with measured support. That choice changes spatial organization even when the number of activated cells is held fixed.
question: Which two zero cells are selected by the local-support ordering?
answer: The two cells with support 0.9 and 0.8 are selected. A random rule may or may not choose the same pair. The exercise compares mechanisms, rather than claiming that one random draw demonstrates universal superiority.
limit: Spatial smoothing can spread artifacts or reinforce existing annotation errors. Support is a prediction assumption, not hidden target evidence. Validate the rule on released-stage holdouts.
variation: Reverse the support vector. Keep the activation count fixed and compare the selected cells again.

title: Normalization and temporal mixing do not commute
concept: Mixing raw counts and then normalizing differs from normalizing each endpoint and then mixing its log expression. Row totals and log1p introduce nonlinearities. These constructions express different assumptions about whether molecules, proportions or logged measurements evolve between stages. A time weight alone does not make them equivalent.
question: Why are the two midpoint vectors different even though both use weight 0.5?
answer: The raw rows [10,0] and [0,1] have different totals. Mixing counts gives the first gene more molecules; normalizing each endpoint first removes that depth difference. Averaging the logs then adds another nonlinear operation.
limit: Neither order is automatically a better biological model. State the modeled quantity and test alternatives without using held-out target measurements.
variation: Set both endpoint row totals equal, then compare the two operations again. Separate the total-count effect from the log effect.

title: A changed observed fraction need not mean population growth
concept: Cell-type proportions depend on which tissue enters the observed field of view. Removing many cells of one type increases another type's fraction without adding a single cell of that second type. Comparing only normalized proportions can conflate developmental growth with dissection, cropping or sampling changes.
question: Did the second population grow when its observed fraction increased?
answer: Its count remains 100. The first population shrinks from 900 observed cells to 90, so the unchanged second population occupies a larger share. Absolute observed counts still do not establish absolute organism-level abundance when sampling changes.
limit: The toy counts describe an observation mechanism. They do not reveal any challenge target's field of view or prescribe a crop for a prediction.
variation: Keep the total observed count fixed and move cells between populations. Explain how that is a different mechanism with a similar proportion change.

title: A negative unbiased MMD estimate can be valid
concept: The population squared kernel distance is nonnegative. Its finite-sample unbiased estimator removes within-sample diagonal terms and can be negative. A biased empirical squared distance includes those terms and behaves differently. Confusing the population quantity with its estimator can cause a valid negative estimate to be incorrectly rejected or silently clipped.
question: Why is the unbiased estimate negative while the biased estimate is nonnegative?
answer: The diagonal correction changes the finite-sample estimate. The script calculates both expressions on two nearby two-point samples and verifies their signs. A negative estimate is not evidence that the population distance is negative.
limit: This uses an explicitly defined one-dimensional Gaussian kernel, not the full official scorer with its fitted representation and bandwidth choices. Do not compare these toy values to board skills.
variation: Move the second sample farther away. Track both estimators while keeping the kernel fixed.

title: A fixed neighbour count changes physical scale with density
concept: A k-nearest-neighbour summary uses a fixed number of cells, not a fixed physical radius. On the same domain, denser sampling makes those neighbours closer. Changing prediction sample size can therefore change the physical scale of a local average even when the underlying tissue distribution is unchanged.
question: How far does a 15-neighbour span extend on increasingly dense unit segments?
answer: The script uses an endpoint and equally spaced positions. Its one-sided 15-step span decreases with sample size. This is a deliberately simple scale calculation, not an exact model of an interior three-dimensional neighbourhood.
limit: Cell count is not a biological size prediction. Sampling and neighbourhood scale are still relevant statistical considerations; use the official scorer for an actual local-metric analysis.
variation: Hold a physical radius fixed instead. Count how many sampled cells fall inside it at each density.

title: Nearly tied eigenvalues make PCA directions unstable
concept: PCA directions are not uniquely determined within a repeated-eigenvalue subspace. A tiny covariance perturbation can rotate the selected leading direction substantially while barely changing the covariance matrix. Registration based on that direction may inherit numerical instability even when the point cloud itself changed very little.
question: How can a tiny perturbation rotate the leading direction by roughly 45 degrees?
answer: The unperturbed covariance has two equal largest eigenvalues. Any orthonormal basis in their plane is valid. The perturbation chooses a different basis; the large axis-angle change does not imply a comparable change in the underlying shape.
limit: An axis sign flip is a separate ambiguity. A stable subspace does not guarantee stable individual axes. This example does not prove an error in any particular scorer.
variation: Replace one leading eigenvalue by 1.2. Repeat the calculation and compare its sensitivity.

title: Rotation alignment needs a determinant constraint
concept: An unconstrained orthogonal least-squares fit may choose a reflection. Proper rotations have determinant +1 and preserve handedness. The determinant correction in a Kabsch-style fit changes the optimization domain, so a reflected target generally cannot have the same perfect fit under proper rotations.
question: Why does the zero-error unconstrained fit have determinant -1?
answer: The synthetic target reflects one coordinate of the source. An orthogonal reflection fits it exactly, while the proper-rotation fit must retain determinant +1 and has nonzero residual error. Translation is irrelevant here because the test isolates the linear part.
limit: Reflection-invariant summaries cannot establish laterality. This numerical example does not certify the handedness sensitivity of any challenge metric.
variation: Generate the target with a known determinant +1 rotation instead of a reflection. Compare both fitted residuals.

title: Linear radius and constant log growth imply different midpoints
concept: Two endpoint sizes do not uniquely identify an intermediate growth law. Linear interpolation in radius and linear interpolation in log radius both fit the endpoints, but produce different middle values. Choosing one is a model assumption and should not be mistaken for information about an unseen specimen.
question: What midpoint follows from each assumption between radii 100 and 400?
answer: Linear radius gives 250. Constant log growth gives the geometric mean, 200. Both calculations are correct under their respective assumptions; neither alone establishes the true intermediate radius.
limit: Published score anchors must not be inverted to recover a hidden size. This exercise uses invented endpoints and does not compute a challenge target property.
variation: Evaluate both curves at fractions 0.25 and 0.75. Explain which assumption makes relative growth constant.

title: Cropping can change RMS radius without biological growth
concept: RMS radius summarizes the observed cloud around its own centroid. A central crop removes distant points and reduces that radius even if every retained position is unchanged. A size trajectory fitted across specimens with different fields of view may partly describe observation rather than growth.
question: Why does the cropped synthetic cloud have a smaller RMS radius?
answer: The crop removes points farther than 1.5 from the original center. The retained cloud is more concentrated. No biological motion or developmental time has been simulated, so the difference is entirely an observation effect.
limit: A central spherical crop is an illustrative mechanism, not a reconstruction of an actual dissection. Field-of-view correction requires evidence beyond this toy example.
variation: Crop only one side and re-center each cloud. Compare the resulting centroid and RMS changes.

title: A common cross-type shift is not automatically technical
concept: A median shift across cell types can separate a shared component from type-specific residuals algebraically. Calling the shared component a technical batch effect requires an additional assumption: broad biological regulation can also be shared. The decomposition alone cannot identify its cause.
question: What shared component is recovered, and which interpretation remains unidentifiable?
answer: In the constructed example the median recovers the component deliberately named technical. Replacing that label with a common biological response leaves the observed numbers unchanged. The numerical recovery is valid; the causal label needs outside evidence.
limit: Removing a shared shift may remove genuine biology. Use matched controls, replication or an explicit model when making a technical interpretation.
variation: Add the same biological effect to all types. Check whether the median-based procedure can distinguish it from a batch effect.

title: A local validation board can reverse official method rankings
concept: A local surrogate is useful for model selection only to the extent that its ordering transfers to the intended evaluation. High local scores alone provide no such evidence. Tie-aware rank comparisons can reveal reversed or uninformative ordering without attempting to reconstruct any hidden target property.
question: What does a Spearman correlation of -1 imply for these four completed predictions?
answer: The local and official orderings reverse exactly, including the tied middle pair. A constant score vector has undefined rank correlation; the script reports null rather than inventing zero agreement or a winner.
limit: Four methods are a small descriptive sample. No significance claim or unseen-score forecast follows. Returned scores may select completed predictions, not reconstruct hidden target measurements.
variation: Change one official score to break a tie. Recompute the ranks rather than assigning arbitrary distinct ranks to equal values.

title: Cell-level splits can share every biological specimen
concept: Splitting cells randomly does not necessarily hold out biological specimens. If cells from the same embryos appear on both sides, shared specimen effects can make generalization look better than it is. Grouped splitting changes the unit of evaluation from cells to the biological group of interest.
question: How many specimen IDs occur on both sides of each split?
answer: The random cell split shares specimen IDs between train and test. The explicit specimen split shares none. Each specimen contains multiple cells, so the number of cells should not be interpreted as the number of independent embryos.
limit: A zero-overlap identifier check cannot prove absence of every form of leakage. It depends on correct metadata and a scientifically appropriate grouping variable.
variation: Make two specimen IDs aliases for the same embryo. Explain why a literal string-overlap check would miss that dependency.

title: Many hyperparameter variants are not independent method families
concept: A table may contain many predictions but only a few distinct modeling families. Strong pooled correlation can reflect between-family differences while saying little about selecting nearby variants within a family. Counting every row as independent overstates the breadth of validation evidence.
question: How do pooled and within-family correlations differ in this synthetic table?
answer: The table deliberately gives each family a strong shared signal and small independent within-family noise. Inspect both summaries. The precise within-family values depend on the seed; their variability is part of the lesson, not a result to optimize away.
limit: Neither a pooled nor a within-family correlation alone establishes generalization. Group structure, sample size, and prospective evaluation matter; do not infer a confidence level from row count.
variation: Increase the number of variants within each family without adding families. Distinguish what information grows and what stays fixed.

title: Every type can increase while aggregate expression decreases
concept: An aggregate expression mean depends on both within-type expression and cell-type proportions. A strong change in mixture can reverse the aggregate direction even when each type changes in the same direction. This is why a pseudobulk shift does not uniquely identify a within-cell response.
question: Why does the aggregate fall when both type means increase?
answer: The mixture moves from mostly high-expression cells to mostly low-expression cells. Its composition effect outweighs the increase within each type. The script displays the type means and the resulting aggregate means so both mechanisms remain visible.
limit: Two invented types illustrate non-identifiability. Real annotations may change across stages, and a missing label need not mean a biologically absent population.
variation: Keep the proportions fixed while retaining the same type means. Compare the aggregate direction with the changing-mixture result.

title: Semantic equality and storage layout are different checks
concept: Arrays can have the same values while using different memory layouts. A digest of a canonical contiguous representation can make their value comparison independent of that layout. A submission-level semantic digest needs more context than the numeric matrix bytes alone.
question: Why do C-order and Fortran-order versions get the same canonical value digest?
answer: The demonstration converts both arrays to the same dtype and contiguous order before hashing. That canonicalization removes the layout difference. It intentionally does not implement a full AnnData semantic hash.
limit: A production digest must also define shape, gene order, cell order, coordinates, sparse duplicate handling, endianness and missing-value behavior. File hashes remain useful for exact artifact identity.
variation: Swap the two gene columns. Explain why a value digest and a gene-labeled semantic digest must be considered separately.

title: An unmeasured gene is different from a measured zero
concept: Zero expression and absence from a measurement panel carry different information. Zero-filling an absent gene makes a rectangular matrix but can hide that distinction. An explicit measurement-status mask retains what was observed, even when the downstream submission contract eventually requires a fixed panel.
question: What information disappears when the absent gene is silently filled with zero?
answer: The two records differ in whether measurement occurred. The numeric zero alone cannot distinguish absence of detected molecules from absence of measurement. The example keeps a boolean measured field and null for the unmeasured value.
limit: A mask does not decide how to impute or whether a source is eligible. Do not silently claim that imputed columns were experimentally measured.
variation: Add a third record whose value is missing because of a processing failure. Design metadata that distinguishes all three cases.

title: Gene-gene structure and spatial structure answer different questions
concept: A gene-pair functional can remain unchanged when entire cell rows are permuted. If coordinates stay fixed, that same permutation changes which expression states are neighbours. An unchanged expression-only structural summary therefore does not establish preserved spatial organization.
question: Which summary is invariant to a common permutation of the expression rows?
answer: The mean gene-pair difference is unchanged because its rowwise values are only reordered. The distance between consecutive expression rows generally changes. Consecutive indices represent a deliberately simple fixed line neighbourhood in this demonstration.
limit: The line-neighbour summary is not the official three-dimensional neighbourhood metric. Use the real scorer and known released coordinates for an actual spatial benchmark.
variation: Permute the coordinates with the expression rows. Explain why the cell-to-position relationship is then preserved.
